words.d: designing tools to fit the human body, here how hands hold a controller or phone
deciding which button or gesture does which action
pressing buttons wildly because you don't know how to control the game
small vibrations that give feedback through the phone or controller
the delay between your input and the result on screen
remembering a press made slightly too early and doing it at the first possible moment

lessons.title: Real humans are playing your game

cards.text: Controls are for real human hands. **If the people who made the game need a special grip to beat it, the controls are wrong, not the players.**

Rogers once found an enemy that could only be beaten by pressing a button incredibly fast. The team used a special grip. Real players couldn't. Thumbs and index fingers do the work. The other fingers mostly just hold on.
The mobile version is "it works on my phone." Developers play on big new phones with practised thumbs. Players use small or cheap phones, with one hand, on a bus, holding coffee in the other.
Playtest on small, cheap phones, one-handed. If a level needs a special technique, your data will show it as a spike of players quitting at that level.
Thumbs steer, index fingers shoot, the rest just hang on.

check.q: Testers can only beat a boss with a special finger grip. What does that mean?
check.why: Controls must fit normal hands. Needing a trick grip is a design failure.

cards.text: Decide control rules up front, so players build muscle memory without thinking. Map controls by **where the hands rest, what the action means, how it looks in real life, and what players already know.**
In PC shooters, the keyboard moves and the mouse aims. Keep keyboard controls clustered around the keys the hand already rests on. You don't need to use every key.
In landscape mobile games, **left thumb moves and right thumb acts.** Brawl Stars, PUBG Mobile, Genshin Impact and Stumble Guys all do this. Don't break it without a very good reason.

Keep combat buttons in an arc around the right thumb's resting spot. Put rare actions, like settings and mail, in the top corners. A common rule: tapping the world means "act", and edge buttons mean "menus".
The 4 Ms: Muscle, Meaning, Mirror, Majority.

check.q: In a landscape action game, what does the left thumb usually do?
check.why: Left thumb moves, right thumb acts. It's the near-universal mobile convention.

lessons.title: Fit the controls to the players

cards.text: Different players have different hands and habits. **Match control complexity to your audience, and let players change the controls when you can.**

- Kids: simple presses, no complex combos.
- PC strategy and shooter fans: let them set their own hotkeys.
- Fighting-game fans love hard inputs, but most players can't do them.
- Never reverse flight controls: pull back to climb.

Track and Field (1983) needed such fast button mashing that players rolled a pencil across the buttons to win. It broke a lot of controllers. If players need a household object to beat your game, your controls failed.

Casual mobile games use one gesture: tap, swipe or drag. Mid-core games let players move, resize and fade buttons. If a clicker needs inhuman tapping, players use auto-tap apps or quit, so add automation as they progress.
The pencil test: needing a pencil to win means the controls failed.

check.q: Who should get the simplest controls?
check.why: Small hands and new players can't do complex combos, so keep it simple.

lessons.title: The dance of the buttons, not mashing

cards.text: Good controls feel like a **dance**: varied, flowing and simple. Controls that are too complex or too repetitive turn into **button mashing**: hitting everything and hoping.

Think about how fingers travel over the controller, not only what happens on screen. Repetitive mashing also hurts: "gamer's thumb" brings stiffness, pain and numbness. Design natural breaks into play.
Brawl Stars has only a move stick, an aim stick, a super and a gadget. Few inputs, lots of expressive variety. That's a dance. In match-3, the dance is swipe, cascade, anticipation, swipe.

The touch version of mashing is frantic tapping everywhere. It happens when players don't know what's tappable or taps give no feedback. Fix it with obvious buttons and instant reactions. Don't block input during long animations.

check.q: Players tap frantically all over the screen. What's the likely cause?
options: They can't tell what's interactive or get no feedback
check.why: Mashing means confusion. Clear buttons and instant feedback fix it.

lessons.title: Never let a button do nothing

cards.text: New players press every button to see what happens, because nobody reads the manual. **Reward that curiosity, and never let a button do nothing.**

Make the character do something cool whenever a button is pressed, even if the player doesn't understand it yet. For buttons that aren't active yet:
- **shrug:** a "nope" sound or animation
- **spotlight:** turn each unlock into a big event, one at a time
- **stand-in:** give the empty button a related action
In Dark Castle, the hero shrugs when he's out of ammo. Brütal Legend stops the game with a full-screen graphic each time you learn a new move.

A locked button should show a lock and wiggle with a soft sound and a note: "Unlocks at level 5". A silent tap feels like a bug. In Survivor.io, simply moving makes your hero destroy enemies, so the first seconds feel great.
Shrug, Spotlight, Stand-in.

check.q: A player taps a locked feature. What's the best response?
options: A lock wiggle and "Unlocks at level 5"
check.why: Every tap needs a response, even if the answer is "not yet".

lessons.title: Make the input mirror the action

cards.text: Controls feel right when **the input copies the action**: the movement, the button's position, or the controls players already know from the genre.
In Pitfall: The Lost Expedition, you push the stick down to dip your canteen in the water and pull it up to drink. In Maximo, high attacks used the top button and low attacks used the bottom button.
Good touch gestures copy real actions: swipe to slice in Fruit Ninja, pull back and release in Angry Birds, flick to throw in Pokémon GO.

Genre conventions are law on mobile: swipe to swap in match-3, drag to merge in merge games, drag a card onto the field in card battlers. Players expect them. Use them unless you have a strong reason not to.
If your gesture doesn't mime the action, ask why not.

check.q: Which control best mirrors its action?
options: Pull back and release to launch a bird
check.why: Pulling back like a slingshot copies the real motion, so it feels natural.

lessons.title: Big and close for urgent, small and far for calm

cards.text: **Big, easy-to-reach inputs get urgent, frequent actions.** Small, harder-to-reach inputs get slow, deliberate ones.
This follows **Fitts's law**: the time to hit a target depends on its distance and size. Close and big is fast. Far and small is slow and error-prone.
On mobile, attack, jump, Play and Collect are big and sit in the thumb zone. Settings, mail, friends and map are smaller and tucked into the top corners, where accidental taps are unlikely.
Keep **danger buttons** (spend gems, sell, delete) away from quick-tap areas, or add a confirm step. A fast thumb should never spend premium currency by accident. That's good design and good ethics.
Big and close for panic, small and far for patience.

check.q: Where should a "Buy for 500 gems" button NOT be?
options: Right next to the quick "Collect" button
check.why: Placing spending next to fast taps causes accidental purchases.

cards.text: Rogers' very important rule: **when the button is pressed, the action must happen.** Nothing angers players faster than waiting for a beautiful animation to finish.

Put the pretty animation at the **end** of the move, as follow-through. When the player presses jump, the only question should be "how high?". Long wind-ups are fine only when the risk pays off with a big reward.
A charge attack is a fair wind-up: hold to charge, release for a big hit. The hold is the risk, the hit is the reward, and the charge is clearly shown.

Touch already has more delay than buttons, so add zero extra. React visually the moment the finger touches: the button presses in, the piece lifts. Let players tap to skip long celebrations, and remember inputs pressed slightly early.
Animation is the bow after the performance, not a speech before it.

check.q: Where should a long, pretty animation go in a jump?
options: At the end, after the jump has started
check.why: The action must start instantly. Polish goes into the follow-through.

lessons.title: Character or camera: pick one and keep it

cards.text: Controls can be **relative to the character** or **relative to the camera.** **Pick one for the whole game and stick with it.** Switching between them confuses everyone.
Character-relative (Rogers' preference): push left, and the character always goes left, wherever the camera faces. Camera-relative: directions follow the camera's view.
Top-down mobile games avoid the problem: the camera never rotates, so up on the joystick is always up on screen. That's one reason fixed cameras are so common in Brawl Stars, Archero and Survivor.io.
3D games with a moving camera, like Genshin Impact and PUBG Mobile, use camera-relative movement. In puzzle and strategy games, never flip the board between levels. Your side stays at the bottom.
Switching mid-game is like handing a driver a mirror.

check.q: Why do many mobile games use a fixed top-down camera?
options: Up on the joystick is always up on screen
Players prefer not seeing their hero
check.why: A fixed camera removes the control confusion of a rotating view.

cards.text: Controllers and phones can talk back with **vibration** and sense motion with a **gyroscope**. Give vibration a **consistent language**, and always tell players about motion controls.
Motion controls are hidden inside the device, so players forget they exist. Show clearly which way to turn or tilt, and remind them the option is there.

A haptic style guide:
- a light tick for selecting
- a medium bump for a match or a hit
- a heavy thud for a big combo
- a success pattern for a win
Use them sparingly.
Always add a vibration toggle, and respect the phone's settings. Some players hate it or play in quiet places. Gyro aiming in mobile shooters should be optional, with invert and sensitivity settings.

check.q: What makes vibration feedback useful instead of annoying?
options: A consistent meaning for each pattern, used sparingly
check.why: Consistent, rare vibrations carry meaning. Constant buzzing is noise.

lessons.title: Motion controls: make them feel real

cards.text: Motion controls work best when they **copy real actions and feel physically right.** Timing, speed and resistance make a virtual sword feel like a sword instead of "floaty".

Tips:
- vary the motions, so arms don't get tired
- prefer broad, simple moves over tiny precise ones
- watch for lag and connection delay
- don't turn every action into a motion
A swipe in Fruit Ninja feels like slicing because the blade trail, the split, the juice and the sound all arrive instantly.

Phones are played in public: on the bus, at work, in bed. Motions that make players look silly are a barrier. Keep physical moves small and optional. In real-time PvP, players blame "bad controls" for bad connections, so show ping clearly.

check.q: Why keep motion controls small on mobile?
options: People play in public and don't want to look silly
check.why: Mobile play happens in public places, so big gestures are awkward.

cards.text: A touchscreen has no buttons to feel, and your finger covers what it touches. **Give each gesture one clear meaning.**

- **Tap:** select, jump, confirm (Flappy Bird).
- **Swipe:** throw, slice, change lane (Subway Surfers).
- **Drag:** move, aim, merge (Clash Royale cards, merge games).
- **Hold:** charge or see details. Hidden, so give a hint.

More gestures:
- **double tap:** a special action, but it can clash with a single tap
- **pinch:** zoom a map or base (Clash of Clans)
- **tilt:** steer or aim. Tiring, and awkward in bed or on the bus
Prefer simple taps and swipes in four directions over complex drawn shapes. Gesture recognition often misreads tiny or complicated motions.

check.q: What's the risk with a hold (long-press) gesture?
options: Players may never discover it without a hint
check.why: Holds are invisible until you try them, so teach them with a hint.

cards.text: Many people hold their phone in one hand and tap with the thumb. **Put frequent actions where the thumb naturally rests: the bottom of the screen.** The top is a stretch.

Joystick types:
- **fixed:** always in the same place, predictable
- **floating:** appears wherever the thumb lands, very forgiving
- **tap-to-move:** tap a destination, great for casual play
- **twin-stick:** left moves, right aims and attacks

In Brawl Stars, tapping the attack button auto-aims at the nearest enemy, while dragging it aims by hand. One control serves both beginners and experts. Among Us lets players choose joystick or tap-to-move.
Hyper-casual and most casual games: one thumb, portrait. Mid-core action and strategy: two thumbs, landscape. Decide early, because it shapes the whole screen layout.

check.q: In one-handed portrait play, where should the main buttons go?
options: Near the bottom, in the thumb's natural zone
check.why: The thumb rests low. The top of the screen is a stretch.

cards.text: Fingers are big and imprecise. **Make touch targets large, and make the game read the player's intent, not exact pixels.**

- Targets at least 44 by 44 points (Apple) or 48 by 48 dp (Android).
- The tap area can be bigger than the drawn icon.
- When dragging, lift the object above the finger and show where it will land.
- Keep controls away from screen edges, where system gestures live.

Forgiveness tricks:
- a drag that ends near a slot snaps into it
- a jump pressed a little early still happens (input buffering)
- a jump pressed just after leaving a ledge still counts ("coyote time")
- auto-aim and auto-attack
Block puzzle games like Block Blast! lift the piece above your fingertip while you drag. Without it, your own finger would hide where the piece goes.

check.q: Why do block puzzle games lift the piece above your finger while dragging?
options: So your finger doesn't hide where it will land
check.why: The finger covers what it touches, so the game moves the object into view.
